title: Indian Restaurant Owners Arrested in Dutch Human Trafficking Probe
excerpt: A Europol-backed inquiry across five EU countries has identified more than 70 potential victims and at least €4 million in suspected profits.
body:
• Indian restaurant owners in the Netherlands have been arrested as part of a human trafficking inquiry, according to DutchNews.nl.
  • The arrests follow a coordinated investigation across five EU countries into the exploitation of workers in Indian restaurants, supported by Europol.
  • Investigators say the inquiry identified more than 70 potential victims and uncovered a trafficking ring that generated at least €4 million in profits.
  • Dutch labour inspectors have separately found undeclared and underpaid workers in Indian restaurants in Amsterdam, The Hague and Almere.

Indian restaurant owners in the Netherlands have been arrested as part of a human trafficking inquiry, DutchNews.nl reported, in a case that has drawn in investigators across five European Union countries. Europol, which supported the coordinated action, said the international investigation identified more than 70 potential victims exploited in Indian restaurants and uncovered a trafficking ring that generated at least €4 million in profits.

Details of the Dutch arrests remain limited, and the inquiry is ongoing. All of those arrested are presumed innocent until proven guilty.

A cross-border investigation

According to Europol, the investigation was a coordinated action spanning five EU countries, targeting the exploitation of workers in Indian restaurants. The agency's announcement describes a trafficking ring operating across borders and generating at least €4 million in profits, with more than 70 potential victims identified.

Europol regularly supports member states in labour exploitation cases by providing operational coordination and analytical support, and the agency's involvement suggests a network operating in multiple jurisdictions rather than an isolated local case.

A sector under scrutiny

The arrests land in a sector that has already been drawing the attention of labour authorities. In a separate recent Europol-supported action against labour exploitation, the Dutch Labour Inspectorate carried out inspections in Indian restaurants in Amsterdam, The Hague and Almere, identifying at least five undeclared employees without valid employment permits. According to reports on that operation, the workers were underpaid and had to work longer hours than permitted.

Restaurants have long been flagged by Dutch authorities as a high-risk sector for labour trafficking, alongside agriculture, construction and domestic work. Enforcement actions have been intensifying across Europe as inspectorates coordinate checks on undeclared work, fraudulent documents and substandard conditions.

Why it matters for the diaspora

Indian restaurants are among the most visible Indian-owned businesses across Europe, and a trafficking case attached to the sector carries reputational weight for the wider diaspora business community — the vast majority of which operates legitimately. At the same time, the potential victims at the centre of the inquiry are themselves largely migrants who came to Europe for work, a reminder that labour exploitation disproportionately strikes the most vulnerable arrivals.

The case also touches a live policy debate in the Netherlands about the enforcement of worker protections and the screening of employer-sponsored migration channels, including how workers recruited from abroad are monitored once they arrive.

What to watch next

With the inquiry ongoing, the next steps will be prosecutorial: whether charges follow the arrests, how many jurisdictions pursue cases, and what support structures are extended to the identified victims. The Videshi will continue to follow this story as official statements emerge.
